sentences.text: The present suit arises from a financial dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant.

The plaintiff asserts that, under the influence and pressure of his wife (the sister of the defendant), he provided a series of financial loans amounting to Rs. 1,04,725/- to the defendant between August 2017 and June 2018.
The plaintiff claims that the defendant, who had agreed to repay the amount within six months, failed to honour this agreement.

Despite several requests and the issuance of a legal notice,
the plaintiff contends that the defendant ignored his calls and ultimately failed to repay the loan,
thereby showing malafide intentions to cheat the plaintiff.

In his defence, the defendant argues that the plaintiff's claims are fabricated and retaliatory in nature, stemming from ongoing personal disputes between the plaintiff and the defendant's sister, Anju, who is the plaintiff's wife.
The defendant denies having received any loan from the plaintiff and, instead, asserts that he lent the plaintiff Rs. 1,50,000/- in cash for personal needs, of which only Rs. 94,850/- was repaid.

The defendant maintains that this suit has been filed by the plaintiff as a tactic to exert pressure during ongoing matrimonial disputes, including a divorce case and a related FIR filed by Anju against the plaintiff under section 498A/406/34 IPC.
CSSCJ/ 1019/2019 Nitish Kumar versus Manish Rana page No. 2 of 31 2.

sentences.text: Pleaded case of the plaintiff is that he is a law-abiding citizen of India and earns his livelihood by lawful means.
The defendant, being the brother-in-law of the plaintiff, approached the plaintiff on several occasions for financial help/loans for his personal needs and requirements.

The plaintiff,
under the influence and pressure of his wife (i.e., the sister of the defendant, Anju), paid the defendant a total amount of Rs. 1,04,725/- (Rupees One Lac Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Only) through multiple bank transfers from his bank account no. 53111047263 at Standard Chartered Bank between August 2017 and June 2018 into the account of the defendant.
7. The defendant had mutually agreed with the plaintiff to repay the above-said friendly loan amount within six months of receiving the last payment/transaction from the plaintiff in June 2018.
After the six-month period, the plaintiff requested several times that the defendant repay the above-said amount.
However, the defendant started ignoring the plaintiff's telephone calls and did not respond regarding the repayment of the aforesaid loan.
Despite the plaintiff's numerous requests, the defendant failed to return the loan amount of Rs. 1,04,725/- (Rupees One Lac Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Only).
All efforts by the plaintiff were in vain.
CSSCJ/ 1019/2019 Nitish Kumar versus Manish Rana page No. 5 of 31 8.

sentences.text: By ignoring the telephonic calls of the plaintiff, the defendant demonstrated his malafide intentions of not repaying a single penny to the plaintiff, which clearly shows his intent to cheat the plaintiff of Rs. 1,04,725/- (Rupees One Lac Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty- Five Only), to which he is legally liable.

The defendant's actions clearly indicate his intention to cheat the plaintiff and commit fraud by withholding the amount of Rs. 1,04,725/- (Rupees One Lac Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Only) as mentioned above.

On 01.08.2019, the plaintiff sent a legal notice dated 30.07.2019 to the defendant, demanding the aforesaid loan amount of Rs. 1,04,725/-
(Rupees One Lac Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Only) through his lawyer by registered post.
However, the defendant has not replied to the legal notice until the date of filing.

9. The facts mentioned above show the clear intentions of the defendant to cheat the plaintiff and commit fraud upon him by withholding an amount of Rs. 1,04,725/- (Rupees One Lac Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Only).

The defendant has unnecessarily harassed, tortured,
and mentally disturbed the plaintiff, who is the sole earner in his family.

sentences.text: 9 39.In his evidence affidavit
Ex. DW-1/A, DW-1, begins by stating that his sister, Anju, was married to the plaintiff, Nitish Kumar, on 12.12.2016.
However, from 13.12.2016, the day after her return to the matrimonial home, Anju was subjected to cruelty by Nitish Kumar and his family.
This continued until Anju was ultimately forced to leave the matrimonial home on 24.06.2019.
According to DW-1, the cruelty stemmed from repeated demands for dowry, Nitish's excessive consumption of alcohol, smoking, and involvement in extramarital affairs.
40.DW-1 further states that despite the birth of a male child, Ayaan, on 03.11.2017, Nitish Kumar failed to provide care or support for either Anju or their child.
This neglect forced Anju to leave the matrimonial home with her child on 25.05.2018.
Subsequently, Anju filed a complaint, No. A-78, on 21.09.2018 with the CAW Cell in Rohini.

Analysis and findings

The issues are adjudicated as under:-
Issue No. (1):-
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to recover a sum of Rs. 1,04,725/- from the defendant which was advanced by the plaintiff as a friendly loan?

but despite repeated requests, the defendant failed to return the said amount.
52.The
plaintiff's case is supported by documentary evidence in the form of bank statements, which reflect the amounts transferred to the defendant's account.
The plaintiff has tendered his evidence via affidavit (Ex. PW-1/A), asserting that the amounts were transferred with the expectation of repayment.
He further alleges that the defendant has malafide intentions to defraud him by withholding the repayment, thereby causing financial distress and mental agony.
53.The defendant, on the other hand, denies the existence of any loan.

He contends that the amount transferred by the plaintiff was not a loan but rather financial support provided for the plaintiff's wife (Anju) and their child during their stay at the defendant's parental home due to matrimonial disputes between the plaintiff and his wife.
The defendant asserts that the plaintiff filed this suit as a means to exert pressure on him and his family amidst ongoing matrimonial disputes between the plaintiff and Anju.

The defendant further claims that the plaintiff had, in fact, borrowed Rs.
1,50,000/- in cash from the defendant's father, Rakesh Rana, on 29.05.2017, of which only Rs.

sentences.text: According to the defendant, the present suit is frivolous and baseless, designed to harass him in retaliation for the plaintiff's personal disputes with his wife.

54.The primary burden of proof lies with the plaintiff under Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act,
1872, to establish that the sum of Rs. 1,04,725/- was indeed advanced as a loan.
In cases where loans are alleged between family members, courts have often required clear evidence of the loan arrangement, especially when the parties are close relatives.
The absence of a written agreement or acknowledgment, coupled with the close familial relationship, casts doubt on the existence of a loan unless there is strong supporting evidence to the contrary.

Where financial assistance is provided in the context of close family relationships, the intention to create a legal obligation to repay the amount must be clearly established by the party claiming the loan.

55.While the plaintiff has produced bank statements as evidence of the transfers made to the defendant, the plaintiff has admitted that there was no written agreement between the parties stipulating the terms of the alleged loan, including the time frame for repayment.

This weakens the plaintiff's position, as the courts typically require more substantial evidence when it comes to proving an oral loan agreement, especially when there is a close familial relationship between the parties.

plaintiff's cross-examination revealed additional weaknesses in his case.
He admitted that the requests for financial assistance were made by both the defendant and his wife, and that he transferred the amounts in an attempt to "save his marriage."
This admission creates ambiguity regarding whether the amounts were advanced as a loan or merely provided to support his wife and child.

The absence of any promissory note, written acknowledgment of debt, or even informal communications (such as emails or messages) further undermines the plaintiff's claim that the amount was a loan intended for repayment.
57.On the other hand, the defendant's defence also suffers from a lack of documentary evidence to support his claim that the plaintiff had borrowed Rs. 1,50,000/- from his father.

However, it is important to note that the burden of proof remains with the plaintiff to establish the loan, and the defendant's inability to substantiate his counterclaims does not absolve the plaintiff of this burden.
58.On the basis of the pleadings, evidence, and applicable legal principles

, it is evident that the plaintiff has failed to discharge the burden of proof to establish that the amount of Rs. 1,04,725/-
was a loan advanced to the defendant.

While the plaintiff has produced evidence of bank transfers,
there is no sufficient documentary or corroborative evidence to show that the transfers were made with the expectation of repayment.

The lack of a CSSCJ/ 1019/2019 Nitish Kumar versus Manish Rana page No. 29 of 31 written agreement, acknowledgment of debt, or communications regarding repayment terms leads to the conclusion that the plaintiff has not sufficiently proven the existence of a loan.

Relief:
63.In light of the foregoing analysis, this Court finds that the plaintiff has failed to establish that the sum of Rs. 1,04,725/- was advanced to the defendant as a friendly loan, and therefore, is not entitled to recover this amount.
